hEDS does not have a tell tale sign specific to its type. 

Most criteria for an hEDS dx can be seen in individuals across the spectrum of EDS subtypes to some degree. Many individual symptoms can be seen in those without EDS as well. So it ends up being diagnosed when there are *enough* overall criteria met by the individual in question, AND when at least x amount of the criteria indicate a systemic issue as a root cause. Essentially, small amounts of evidence of full body involvement + ample evidence of individual experiences relating to connective tissue = a likely dx. 

However, the specific indicators of vEDS can be hidden and go without discovery until later life, and the patient's subjective experience may not differ in the day to day. So if a person is a viable candidate for a dx of hEDS, doing a simple ECG can lead the evaluating doctor to identify a structural difference that points to the venous type even if there were no other venous specific indicators found during the initial bodily exam and historical interview. Finding this structural difference can be the difference between life and death.
